response:
## The problem

Our team of twelve ships slower every quarter, and long-lived feature branches are a major cause. Branches that live for weeks drift from main, and merging them back triggers conflicts that eat entire days. Two problems keep recurring:

- Integration happens only at the end, so defects surface late, when they are expensive to fix.
- Engineers avoid refactoring shared code because it collides with open branches, so technical debt piles up.

Meanwhile, CI tests branches in isolation, so a green build tells us little about whether main will actually work once everything lands.

## The proposal

I propose trunk-based development: every engineer commits small, reviewed changes directly to main at least daily, using feature flags for incomplete work. Concretely:

- Cap branch lifetime at one working day, enforced by a CI check.
- Gate unfinished work behind flags so main stays releasable at every commit, backed by a stronger automated test suite.
- Pilot this with two sub-teams for two weeks before rolling out to everyone.

This shortens feedback loops, keeps main deployable, and removes the merge-conflict tax we pay on nearly every release.

## What could go wrong

The strongest objection is real: trunk-based development demands discipline and tooling we don't fully have. Without solid flags and a fast, trustworthy test suite, "always deployable" can become "always broken," and someone could ship half-finished logic to production by accident. This isn't a strawman - teams have adopted this prematurely and been burned. The honest answer is that this proposal is only as safe as our investment in flags, tests, and fast code review; if we won't fund that, we shouldn't do this yet.

There's also a cultural risk: engineers used to isolated branches may resist exposing unfinished work daily until they see the process work.

I would like a decision by the end of next week.
